text: Wular Lake, known in Urdu as [ʋʊlər] and in Kashmiri as [ʋɔlar], is one of the largest freshwater lakes in the Indian subcontinent, located near Bandipora town in the Bandipora district of Jammu and Kashmir, India. It was formed due to tectonic activity and is fed by the Jhelum River, along with the Madhumati and Arin streams. The lake's area fluctuates seasonally between 30 and 189 square kilometres, with significant portions drained due to willow plantations built along its shores in the 1950s. Historically, it was referred to as Mahapadmasar in Sanskrit, mentioned in the Nilamata Purana, and known as Ullola due to the high leaping waves it produces in the afternoons, a name believed to have evolved into Wulor or Wular over time. The Kashmiri word 'Wul,' meaning a gap or fissure, reflects its origin from a natural fissure. Sultan Zain-ul-Abidin is credited with constructing an artificial island, Zaina Lank, in the lake in 1444. According to local tradition, a city ruled by King Raja Sudrasen was submerged by the lake due to his crimes, and during winter, ruins of a submerged temple were said to appear. Zain-ul-Abidin sank a barge, built a foundation of bricks and stones on it, erected a mosque and other structures, and named the islet Lanka, using the proceeds from the discovery of two solid gold idols. The lake supports diverse fish species, including common carp (Cyprinus carpio), rosy barb (Barbus conchonius), mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), Nemacheilus species, Crossocheilus latius, and snowtrout species such as Sattar snowtrout (Schizopyge curvifrons), Chirruh snowtrout (Schizopyge esocinus), Schizothorax planifrons, Schizothorax macropogon, Schizothorax longipinus, and Chush snowtrout (Schizopyge niger). It also hosts a rich variety of birds, including black-eared kite, Eurasian sparrowhawk, short-toed eagle, Himalayan golden eagle, Himalayan monal, chukar partridge, koklass pheasant, rock dove, common cuckoo, alpine swift, Indian roller, Himalayan woodpecker, hoopoe, barn swallow, and golden oriole. Local communities harvest aquatic plants like Phragmites and Nymphoides for food and animal feed. Fish from the lake form a major part of the diet for thousands in the Kashmir Valley, with over eight thousand fishermen relying on it, primarily catching endemic Schizothorax species and non-native carp, which account for about 60 percent of the total fish yield in Kashmir. Hundreds of villagers are employed by cooperative societies involved in trading the catch. The Government of India Tourism, in collaboration with Kerala Tourism and J&K Tourism, launched boating, water sports, and water skiing at the lake, with operations beginning in September 2011. Wular Lake is one of 80 Indian wetlands designated as a Ramsar site and was recognized as a Wetland of National Importance in 1986 and as a Wetland of International Importance in 1990 under the Ramsar Convention. Despite this, the lake faces environmental threats such as agricultural expansion in its catchment areas, pollution from fertilizers and animal waste, hunting of birds, and weed infestation. Waste has accumulated along the shores and in the water, making parts of the lake shallow and covered in mud and garbage, reducing its size and depth. The Environment Ministry approved Rs 4 billion for a restoration project under the National Lake Conservation Programme, scheduled to begin in December 2011 and lasting 5 to 10 years, involving the cutting of two million trees. The South Asian Voluntary Association of Environmentalists (SAVE) is a joint initiative aimed at protecting the lake's ecology. The Tulbul Lock Project, an under-construction river navigation and water level control structure at the lake's mouth, is 439 feet (134 m) long and 40 feet (12 m) wide with a maximum storage capacity of 300,000 acre⋅ft (370×10^6 m³). It aims to maintain a minimum water depth of 4.5 feet (1.4 m) in the river up to Baramulla during the lean winter months, with enhanced inflows from the Kishanganga River via the Kishanganga Hydroelectric Plant. The project was conceived in the early 1980s and work started in 1984, with average annual inflows or outflows of nearly 7 billion cubic meters. Between 1987 and 2025, India and Pakistan disputed the project, with Pakistan objecting in 1987 on the grounds that it violated the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), leading India to halt construction. India maintains that the project complies with paragraphs 7(c) and 9 of Annexure E of the IWT, while Pakistan argues that storage above 10,000 acre-feet (12×10^6 m³) for non-power purposes constitutes a violation. India claims the suspension harmed the people of Jammu and Kashmir and deprived Pakistan of potential irrigation and power benefits. In 2025, India suspended the IWT, allowing the revival of the Tulbul project, and also accelerated work on the Chenab-Ravi-Beas-Sutlej Link Canal (200 km long with 12 tunnels), increasing the capacity of major dams like Uri, Dulhasti, Salal, Baglihar, Nimu Bajgo, and Chutak, and constructing new dams such as Kishanganga, Ratle, and Pakal Dul. The lake's storage capacity will be expanded to 300,000 acre-feet or more, up to 1580 m MSL, by treating it as a reservoir for a run-of-the-river (RoR) hydro power plant with a low-head (nearly 8 meters) power plant. The deepened river bed level at the dam's toe will be below 1,570 m (5,151 ft) MSL for a 4,000 cusecs flow. A RoR power plant with sluice gates would help flush sediment from the lake. The enlarged lake would fully meet downstream navigational needs during lean flow seasons. Regulated water storage in the lake would significantly boost power generation from downstream projects such as the Lower Jhelum (105 MW), Uri (720 MW), proposed Kohala (1124 MW), Azad Pattan (720 MW), Mahl (590 MW), and Karot (720 MW) in Pakistan, although its own power generation remains marginal.
